provisions_triggered.name: Due Process / Law of the Land

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: The court reversed a termination of parental rights because the trial court never prescribed written norms of parental conduct the father was expected to meet, and it announced prospectively that a termination-seeking party must prove parental potential for harm by clear and convincing evidence.
key_cases.relevance: C.G. is the source of Oklahoma's clear-and-convincing standard for termination and of the pre-termination notice requirement that governs every TPR appeal.
key_cases.quote: Judicial clarity in the prescribed norms of parental conduct is essential to the preservation of the procedural safeguards mandated by state and federal due process.

key_cases.holding: The court held that a parent whose child has been adjudicated deprived is entitled to a jury trial in a State-initiated proceeding to terminate parental rights under Okla. Const. art. 2, § 19, overruling contrary prior decisions.
key_cases.relevance: A.E. is the foundational Oklahoma holding that a parent facing State-sought termination has a constitutional right to trial by jury.
key_cases.quote: We find that parental rights are too precious to be terminated without the full panoply of protections afforded by the Oklahoma Constitution.

key_cases.holding: The court reinstated a jury verdict terminating a mother's parental rights, holding that clear and convincing evidence showed she failed to correct the substance-abuse conditions and that termination served the child's best interests.
key_cases.relevance: Daniels is the modern Oklahoma Supreme Court restatement of the clear-and-convincing best-interests standard for termination.
key_cases.quote: In parental termination cases, the State must show by clear and convincing evidence that the child's best interest is served by the termination of parental rights.

key_cases.case_name: In the Matter of the Adoption of M.A.S.
key_cases.holding: The court reversed an order declaring a child eligible for adoption without the biological father's consent because the record lacked clear and convincing evidence that his partial nonpayment of support was willful or that he had the ability to pay in full.
key_cases.relevance: M.A.S. is the current Oklahoma Supreme Court statement of the proof required to sever a parent's consent right and clear the path to a stepparent adoption.
key_cases.quote: unless the trial court's determination rests on clear and convincing evidence, that determination will be reversed

key_cases.court: Court of Civil Appeals of Oklahoma
key_cases.holding: The court reversed the termination of an incarcerated father's parental rights because the record contained no clear and convincing evidence supporting the statutory grounds alleged against him.
key_cases.relevance: Khan is the Oklahoma authority for the proposition that incarceration alone, without record proof of the statutory elements, cannot terminate parental rights.
key_cases.quote: We hold that the record does not include clear and convincing evidence supporting termination in this case and reverse.

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held that New York's fair-preponderance standard for permanent neglect proceedings violates the Due Process Clause, and that before a State may irrevocably sever the rights of parents in their natural child it must support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence.
key_cases.relevance: It is the federal constitutional floor for every termination of parental rights, including those litigated under Oklahoma's Children's Code.
key_cases.quote: due process requires that the State support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence

key_cases.case_name: In the Matter of A.M. and R.W.
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed a jury termination verdict, reviewing the procedural due process claim de novo and holding that a parent may be excluded from the courtroom during a child's testimony only on a showing at a hearing of significant emotional harm, but that this mother showed no impairment of her defense.
key_cases.relevance: A.M. and R.W. supplies the Oklahoma Supreme Court's de novo standard of review for procedural due process challenges to a termination trial and the limits on excluding a parent from the child's testimony.
key_cases.quote: a parent should not be excluded from the courtroom absent a showing at a hearing that the child would suffer significant emotional harm caused by the parent's presence

key_cases.holding: The court reversed the termination of an unwed father's parental rights, holding he was denied due process because he was never given adequate notice of the pregnancy and birth and there was no clear and convincing evidence supporting termination under the adoption statute.
key_cases.relevance: K.P.M.A. is the controlling Oklahoma Supreme Court authority on the notice a biological father is constitutionally owed before his consent right can be severed to clear an adoption.
key_cases.quote: Father had a right, under the Due Process Clause, to notice of the fact that Mother was pregnant with his child.

key_cases.case_name: In the Matter of the Adoption of R.W.S.
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed the denial of a non-relative couple's adoption petition, holding that where a court order deferred the father's child support there was no clear and convincing evidence of a willful failure to support that would make the child eligible for adoption without his consent.
key_cases.relevance: R.W.S. is part of the controlling Oklahoma Supreme Court line fixing the clear-and-convincing burden and the willfulness element before a father's consent right can be severed for nonsupport.
key_cases.quote: The standard of proof in determining a child's eligibility for adoption without parental consent is clear and convincing evidence.

extended_foster_care_age: Up to age 21 (voluntary; conditions apply; began 1 July 2026; 10A O.S. § 1-7-112a)

common_failures: Failure to prove unfitness by clear and convincing evidence
Santosky v. Kramer standard not met

timeline_requirements.deadline: 6 months, then every 6 months thereafter; 30 days after a court determination that reasonable efforts to return the child are not required
timeline_requirements.starts_from: Child enters out-of-home placement — the earlier of the adjudication date or 60 days after the child is removed from the home

timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Must file TPR or document compelling reason
